nameStory: The 'small-flowered' in this buttercup's name tells the whole story - its tiny yellow petals are so minuscule they almost look like they forgot to fully develop! The scientific name 'abortivus' comes from Latin meaning 'to pass away,' possibly referring to these underwhelming petals that seem to have given up halfway through growing. It's like the wallflower of the buttercup family - present but not trying to steal the show.
description: Small-flowered buttercup is a modest woodland wildflower that reaches about 1-3 feet tall with branching stems. Unlike its flashy buttercup cousins with their shiny yellow petals, this one produces tiny, almost forgettable pale yellow flowers that are barely larger than a pinky nail. The plant has distinctive kidney-shaped basal leaves and deeply-lobed stem leaves that help make up for its unremarkable blooms. It's one of those plants you might walk past without noticing, but once you know what to look for, you'll spot it everywhere in New England's woodlands.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale yellow flowers with 5 petals so small they look stunted - each petal barely reaches 1-2mm long and often shorter than the green sepals beneath them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two distinct leaf types: rounded, kidney-shaped basal leaves with scalloped edges, and deeply-cut stem leaves with 3-5 narrow lobes that feel thin and delicate

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, branching stems 1-3 feet tall that feel smooth and somewhat succulent when gently squeezed, often growing in small colonies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small clusters of tiny, flattened seed heads that look like miniature bunches of flat green teardrops arranged in a small ball

habitat: Small-flowered buttercup thrives in moist, rich soils of deciduous and mixed woodlands throughout New England, often in partially shaded areas along woodland edges, clearings, and disturbed forest floors. You'll frequently find it in the same areas as trout lily, wild ginger, and other spring woodland wildflowers, particularly where the soil stays consistently moist but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: Blooms from April through June with its tiny yellow flowers, often starting before the forest canopy fully leafs out. The distinctive kidney-shaped basal leaves emerge early and are most prominent during this season.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming into early summer while developing its small clustered seed heads. The deeply-lobed stem leaves are fully developed and the plant reaches its full height.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse, while the delicate foliage begins to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground parts, leaving no above-ground traces until the following spring.

funFact: Small-flowered buttercup is essentially the 'stealth bomber' of wildflowers - despite having the most underwhelming blooms in the entire buttercup family, it's actually one of the most widespread and successful buttercups in North America, found from coast to coast and thriving while its showier cousins struggle in many habitats!
confusionNotes: The tiny, pale flowers immediately separate this from all other buttercups in New England, which have much larger, brighter yellow petals. The kidney-shaped basal leaves are also unique among our local buttercups. Memory trick: 'Small-flowered = small flowers' - if the yellow petals are barely visible, you've found your plant!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'buttercup' fool you into expecting the classic bright, shiny yellow flowers you associate with the family - this species breaks all the buttercup rules with its modest appearance. The term 'crowfoot' in some of its alternate names refers to the deeply-lobed stem leaves that supposedly resemble a crow's foot.
compareHints: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers. Early buttercup blooms around the same time but has typical bright yellow petals, while creeping and meadow buttercups have large, glossy yellow flowers. The kidney-shaped basal leaves also distinguish it from the more deeply-divided basal leaves of most other buttercup species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.
Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
